newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Delegates deadlocked on final Earth Summit statement.
newsitem.headline: Delegates deadlocked on final Earth Summit statement.

text.p: Rich and poor countries, island states and oil-exporting nations were still deadlocked on several key issues on Friday as they struggled to agree on a final document from the U.N. Earth Summit.
The meeting, which worked most of Thursday night, is due to end at midnight EDT (0400 GMT).

But officials said discussions by the 173 delegations could last through Friday night because of differences on such topics as global warming and financial targets for helping poor countries meet environmental goals.
"The session went until 5 a.m. this morning. and there was even talk of a session on Saturday," said U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard.
Among the controversial issues, only forest protection was agreed, with Canadian and European proposals for a binding treaty shot down by the summit and shelved for several years.
The week-long gathering of presidents, prime ministers and environment ministers that began on Monday is supposed to give a report card on the landmark 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.
It should set guidelines for the next century on "sustainable development"-- the pairing of ecological objectives with economic growth.
But critics were already slamming this meeting as a failure.

"It's a betrayal of Rio," said Gordon Shepherd of the World Wide Fund for Nature. "The real horror is that many cities and towns are implementing Rio decisions without international support. They came here for inspiration and they got nothing."

Even a 26-point political statement, the results of several rounds of consultations before the session began, may be thrown out because of differences on several issues, including objectives for increasing foreign aid, delegates said.
President Bill Clinton, in a summit speech late on Thursday, dwelt at length on the hazards of global warming and promised to educate the American people on the need to reduce carbon emissions.
But many environmentalists were deeply disappointed he did not present a specific plan to reduce so-called greenhouse gases from fossil fuels, like, as the European Union has done.
Among the main issues under discussion for the final document:
--ATMOSPHERE:

The European Union proposed a 15 percent reduction in emissions below the 1990 level by 2010. Small island states, threatened with being swamped by rising seas because of global warming, wanted a much higher reduction. The United States, Japan and Australia want no specific targets at this time, preferring to wait for a December conference on the topic in Kyoto, Japan. The final document will probably call for "realistic targets" by the year 2010.
-- FINANCIAL AID:

Most industrial countries pledged at Rio to increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of their gross national product, a goal on the U.N. agenda since 1972. But aid has fallen to below 0.3 percent, especially in the United States.
The United States, Germany and others are objecting to goals for individual countries to reverse the trend of development aid by 2002.
A European Union proposal for an aviation fuel tax was shot down by opposition from the United States, Japan and oil-producing countries such as Venezuela, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia.
- -FORESTS:

Canada and the European Union lost out on their proposal to start negotiations on a forest treaty that was to have introduced standards for the logging trade. Instead the issue of a treaty would be considered again in 2000. If a decision was made then it would take another five years to formulate a treaty.

The United States, Brazil and India as well as most environmental groups opposed a treaty, preferring first to see existing agreement enforced. In the meantime discussions among governments will continue to monitor compliance with existing non-binding regulations.
